Saturn is so low-density that it would float in a bathtub large enough to hold it.
Sunlight takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach Earth.

The Great Red Spot on Jupiter is a storm that has been raging continuously for at least 350 years.
Space is completely silent, because sound needs a medium like air to travel, and space is a near-vacuum.
The International Space Station travels at about 28,000 km/h, circling Earth roughly every 90 minutes.
Olympus Mons on Mars is the largest volcano in the solar system — nearly three times the height of Mount Everest.

The asteroid belt's total mass is less than that of Earth's Moon, despite containing millions of individual objects.

physics_lab.title: Astrophysics Lab
physics_lab.subtitle: Real formulas. Real numbers. Try it before you're told the answer.

escape_velocity.title: Escape Velocity
escape_velocity.prompt: How fast would something need to travel to permanently escape a planet's gravity?
escape_velocity.formula_explainer: This comes from balancing kinetic energy against gravitational potential energy. G is the gravitational constant, M is the planet's mass, and R is its radius from the center.

q1.prompt: If a planet has the same mass as Earth but twice its radius, what happens to its escape velocity?
q1.explain: Escape velocity is inversely proportional to the square root of radius, so a bigger planet of the same mass has a lower escape velocity — gravity is spread over a larger surface.

q2.prompt: What does the escape velocity formula NOT depend on?
q2.opt1: The planet's mass
q2.explain: v = √(2GM/R) depends only on mass and radius — not on launch direction, since it's a scalar minimum speed.

q3.prompt: Why is Jupiter's escape velocity so much higher than Earth's?
q3.opt2: Jupiter is closer to the Sun
q3.explain: Jupiter's huge mass (about 318 Earths) dominates the formula, giving it a far higher escape velocity (~59.5 km/s) despite also having a much larger radius.

q4.prompt: If you could double a planet's mass while keeping its radius the same, what happens to escape velocity?
q4.explain: Since v ∝ √M, doubling mass multiplies escape velocity by √2 (about 1.41×), not by 2.

q5.prompt: Does escape velocity depend on the mass of the object trying to escape (like a rocket)?
q5.opt1: Yes, heavier rockets need higher escape velocity
q5.opt2: No, it's the same for any object regardless of its own mass
q5.opt3: Only for objects heavier than 1000 kg
q5.explain: Escape velocity comes from energy balance where the escaping object's mass cancels out of the equation — it's the same for a pebble or a spacecraft.

q6.prompt: The Moon's escape velocity is about 2.4 km/s, much lower than Earth's 11.2 km/s. Why?
q6.opt1: The Moon has far less mass and a smaller radius than Earth
q6.opt3: The Moon is farther from the Sun
q6.explain: The Moon's much smaller mass (about 1.2% of Earth's) reduces GM far more than its smaller radius increases escape velocity, giving a much lower net value.

escape_velocity.challenge_label: Match Mars's real escape velocity: 5.03 km/s

orbital_velocity.title: Orbital Velocity
orbital_velocity.prompt: How fast does something need to move sideways to stay in a stable circular orbit, without falling in or flying away?
orbital_velocity.formula_explainer: This balances the centripetal force needed for circular motion against gravity's pull. It depends on mass and radius similarly to escape velocity — in fact orbital velocity always equals escape velocity divided by √2.
orbital_velocity.sanity_check: Real value for the ISS (~400 km altitude): ≈ 7.7 km/s

q1.prompt: How does orbital velocity compare to escape velocity at the same distance?
q1.opt2: It's the same as escape velocity
q1.explain: Escape velocity is exactly √2 times orbital velocity at any given radius — this falls directly out of comparing the two formulas.

q2.prompt: The International Space Station orbits at about 400 km altitude. Why doesn't it fall to Earth?
q2.opt1: It's moving sideways fast enough that its fall matches Earth's curvature
q2.opt2: There's no gravity at that altitude
q2.opt3: Its engines constantly push it upward
q2.explain: Orbit is really continuous falling — the ISS moves sideways at ~7.7 km/s, fast enough that as it falls, the ground curves away at the same rate.

q3.prompt: If a satellite orbits closer to Earth, what happens to its required orbital velocity?
q3.explain: Since v = √(GM/r), a smaller orbital radius r means a larger orbital velocity is needed to maintain the orbit.

q4.prompt: Geostationary satellites orbit much higher (~35,786 km) than the ISS. Is their orbital velocity higher or lower?
q4.explain: At a much larger radius, orbital velocity is lower — geostationary satellites move at about 3.1 km/s, versus the ISS's 7.7 km/s.

q5.prompt: What provides the centripetal force that keeps a satellite in orbit?
q5.opt1: Gravity from the body it orbits
q5.explain: Gravity itself supplies exactly the centripetal force needed for circular motion at the correct orbital velocity — no continuous thrust is required.

q6.prompt: Orbital velocity around the Sun at Earth's distance is about 29.8 km/s. What does this represent?
q6.opt1: How fast Earth spins on its axis
q6.opt2: How fast Earth travels around the Sun
q6.explain: 29.8 km/s is Earth's orbital velocity around the Sun — the speed needed to maintain a stable orbit at 1 AU.

orbital_velocity.challenge_label: Match a geostationary satellite's orbital velocity: 3.07 km/s

kepler.title: Kepler's Third Law
kepler.prompt: How does a planet's distance from the Sun relate to how long its year is?
kepler.formula_explainer: Discovered by Johannes Kepler in 1619: the square of a planet's orbital period equals the cube of its distance, when period is in years and distance is in AU around the Sun.
kepler.sanity_check: Real value for Mars (1.52 AU): ≈ 1.88 years

q1.prompt: A planet orbits the Sun at 4 AU. Roughly how long is its year?
q1.explain: T² = a³, so T² = 4³ = 64, and T = √64 = 8 years.

q2.prompt: Which planet has a longer year: one closer to the Sun, or one farther away?
q2.opt1: The one farther away
q2.explain: T² ∝ a³ means greater distance always means a longer orbital period — farther planets take longer to complete one orbit.

q3.prompt: Mercury orbits at about 0.39 AU. Roughly how long is its year?
q3.explain: T² = 0.39³ ≈ 0.059, so T ≈ √0.059 ≈ 0.24 years — matching Mercury's real 88-day year closely.

q4.prompt: Kepler's Third Law in this simple form (T² = a³) works exactly for which case?
q4.opt1: Only objects orbiting the Sun, with T in years and a in AU
q4.opt2: Any two orbiting objects anywhere in the universe
q4.explain: This simplified form only holds for objects orbiting the Sun with those specific units — a more general version includes both masses for other systems.

q5.prompt: Why was Kepler's Third Law historically important?
q5.opt1: It gave the first mathematical relationship connecting orbital distances and times, later explained by Newton's gravity
q5.opt2: It proved the Sun was the center of the universe with no exceptions
q5.opt3: It disproved the existence of comets
q5.explain: Kepler's laws described planetary motion precisely from observation, and later became a cornerstone that Newton's theory of gravity successfully explained from first principles.

q6.prompt: A hypothetical planet takes 27 years to orbit the Sun. Roughly how far out is it (in AU)?

kepler.challenge_label: Match Jupiter's real orbital period: 11.86 years (try 5.2 AU)

inverse_square.title: Inverse-Square Law of Light
inverse_square.prompt: How much dimmer does a star look if you're twice as far away from it?
inverse_square.formula_explainer: A star's brightness falls off with the square of distance — double the distance, and you get only a quarter of the light, because the same light spreads over 4 times the area.
inverse_square.sanity_check: At 2× the distance, brightness drops to 25% of the original.

q1.prompt: If you triple your distance from a star, how much dimmer does it appear?
q1.explain: Brightness falls with the square of distance, so 3× the distance means 3² = 9 times dimmer.

q2.prompt: Two identical stars are the same actual brightness, but Star A looks dimmer than Star B from Earth. What does this most likely tell you?
q2.opt1: Star A is farther away
q2.explain: For stars of identical true brightness (luminosity), the inverse-square law means the dimmer-looking one is simply farther away — this is actually how astronomers estimate distances using 'standard candles'.

q3.prompt: If you move to 4 times the distance from a light source, how much of the original brightness remains?
q3.explain: Brightness falls with the square of distance: at 4× distance, brightness is 1/4² = 1/16 of the original.

q4.prompt: Why does the inverse-square law involve an area (4πd²) in its formula?
q4.opt1: Light spreads out over an ever-larger sphere as it travels, and that sphere's surface area grows with distance squared
q4.opt3: It's just a mathematical convenience with no physical meaning
q4.explain: Light radiates outward in all directions, spreading over the surface of an expanding sphere. Since a sphere's surface area is 4πd², the same total light gets diluted over an area that grows with d².

q5.prompt: This same inverse-square pattern also applies to which other force?
q5.explain: Gravity also follows an inverse-square law (F ∝ 1/r²) — it's one of several fundamental phenomena in physics that spread outward the same geometric way.

q6.prompt: Astronomers use the inverse-square law with 'standard candles' (stars of known true brightness) mainly to measure what?
q6.explain: By comparing a standard candle's known true brightness to how dim it appears, astronomers can calculate distance directly from the inverse-square relationship.

inverse_square.challenge_label: Find the distance where brightness drops to exactly 25%

wien.title: Wien's Law
wien.prompt: What color does an object glow, based purely on its temperature?
wien.formula_explainer: Wien's Law says the wavelength at which an object radiates most strongly is inversely proportional to its temperature. Hotter objects peak at shorter (bluer) wavelengths; cooler objects peak at longer (redder) ones.
wien.sanity_check: The Sun (~5,778 K) peaks at about 501 nm — in the visible blue-green part of the spectrum.

q1.prompt: As an object gets hotter, what happens to its peak wavelength?
q1.explain: Wien's Law is an inverse relationship — higher temperature means shorter peak wavelength, which is why very hot stars look blue-white.

q2.prompt: A star with a surface temperature of about 3,000 K would appear mostly what color?
q2.opt1: Red
q2.explain: Cooler stars (like red dwarfs, around 2,500–3,700 K) peak at longer, redder wavelengths according to Wien's Law.

q3.prompt: A star with a surface temperature of about 20,000 K would appear mostly what color?
q3.explain: Hot stars (B-type, 10,000–30,000 K) peak at short wavelengths, appearing blue-white — the opposite end of the spectrum from cool red stars.

q4.prompt: Wien's Law uses the constant b ≈ 2,897,771 nm·K. What role does this constant play?
q4.opt1: It converts temperature directly into peak wavelength via division
q4.opt2: It has no real physical meaning, just a scaling number
q4.opt3: It only applies to the Sun specifically
q4.explain: Wien's displacement constant (b) is a universal physical constant — dividing it by any temperature in Kelvin gives that object's peak emission wavelength.

q5.prompt: Does Wien's Law apply only to stars?
q5.opt1: No — it applies to any object that radiates as a blackbody, including planets and even human bodies
q5.opt2: Yes, it only works for stars
q5.opt3: It only works for objects hotter than the Sun
q5.explain: Wien's Law is a general blackbody radiation law. It's why thermal cameras can detect the infrared glow of comparatively cool objects like human bodies, which peak in infrared, not visible light.

q6.prompt: If a star's peak wavelength shifts to be shorter over time, what has likely happened to its temperature?
q6.opt3: Temperature and peak wavelength are unrelated
q6.explain: Wien's Law is an inverse relationship — a shift to shorter (bluer) peak wavelength means the object has gotten hotter.

wien.challenge_label: Match Betelgeuse's approximate peak wavelength: ~828 nm (try ~3,500 K)

stefan_boltzmann.title: Stefan–Boltzmann Law
stefan_boltzmann.prompt: How bright is a star, really, based on its size and temperature?
stefan_boltzmann.formula_explainer: A star's total light output (luminosity) depends on both its surface area and temperature. Since L ∝ R²T⁴, temperature matters enormously — doubling temperature increases luminosity 16-fold.
stefan_boltzmann.sanity_check: At Sun-like radius and temperature (1× each), luminosity should read almost exactly 1.

q1.prompt: If you double a star's temperature while keeping its radius the same, how much brighter does it get?
q1.explain: Luminosity depends on T⁴, so doubling temperature increases luminosity by 2⁴ = 16 times.

q2.prompt: If you double a star's radius while keeping its temperature the same, how much brighter does it get?
q2.opt1: 2 times
q2.explain: Luminosity depends on R², so doubling radius increases luminosity by 2² = 4 times.

q3.prompt: A red giant is cooler than the Sun but far more luminous. How is this possible?
q3.opt1: Its enormous radius more than makes up for its lower temperature
q3.opt2: It's actually hotter than it looks
q3.opt3: Red giants don't follow the Stefan-Boltzmann law
q3.explain: Since luminosity depends on R², a huge radius can outweigh a lower T⁴ term — this is exactly why red giants, despite cooler surfaces, shine far brighter than the Sun.

q4.prompt: Why does temperature (T⁴) affect luminosity so much more strongly than radius (R²)?
q4.opt1: Because it's raised to the 4th power instead of the 2nd, so small temperature changes compound faster
q4.opt2: Temperature doesn't really affect luminosity much at all
q4.opt3: This is only true for stars, not other objects
q4.explain: A 4th-power relationship grows far faster than a squared one — this is a general feature of blackbody radiation, not unique to stars.

q5.prompt: Two stars have the same luminosity. One is much hotter. What must be true of the hotter one?
q5.opt1: It must have a smaller radius
q5.opt2: It must have a larger radius
q5.explain: Since L ∝ R²T⁴, if luminosity is equal but T is higher, R must be smaller to balance the equation — this is exactly how white dwarfs (hot, tiny) can match the luminosity of larger, cooler stars.

stefan_boltzmann.challenge_label: Find settings where luminosity is 16× the Sun's

physics_lab.challenge_hint: Adjust the sliders until your result matches the target.

doppler_shift.title: Doppler Shift
doppler_shift.prompt: How does a star's motion toward or away from us change the light we see?
doppler_shift.formula_explainer: As a star moves away, its light stretches to longer (redder) wavelengths; moving toward us, it compresses to shorter (bluer) ones. This is the same physics behind the radial velocity method for finding exoplanets.
doppler_shift.sanity_check: A star moving away at 20 km/s shifts a 500nm line by only about 0.033 nm — tiny, but precisely measurable.
doppler_shift.challenge_label: Match the shift for a star receding at 100 km/s

q1.prompt: A star's light shifts toward longer, redder wavelengths. What does this tell you?
q1.opt1: The star is moving away from us
q1.opt2: The star is moving toward us
q1.explain: A shift to longer wavelengths (redshift) means the source is moving away — the same effect as a car horn dropping in pitch as it drives away.

q2.prompt: What everyday phenomenon works on the same principle as the Doppler shift?
q2.opt1: A siren changing pitch as an ambulance passes
q2.explain: The Doppler effect applies to any wave, including sound — a siren sounds higher-pitched approaching and lower-pitched receding, exactly like light shifting blue or red.

angular_size.title: Angular Size
angular_size.prompt: How big does an object appear in the sky, based on its real size and distance?
angular_size.formula_explainer: An object's apparent size in the sky depends on both its true size and how far away it is — a small nearby object can look the same size as a huge distant one.
angular_size.sanity_check: The Moon and Sun have almost the same angular size from Earth (~0.5°) despite the Sun being 400× larger — because it's also about 400× farther away, which is why total solar eclipses are possible.
angular_size.challenge_label: Match the Moon's real angular size: about 0.52°

q1.prompt: Why do the Sun and Moon appear almost the same size in Earth's sky?
q1.opt1: The Sun is about 400× larger but also about 400× farther away
q1.opt2: They are actually the same physical size
q1.opt3: It's an optical illusion with no real explanation
q1.explain: This near-perfect coincidence in ratios is exactly what makes total solar eclipses — where the Moon precisely covers the Sun — possible.

q2.prompt: If two objects have the same angular size, what must be true?
q2.opt1: Their true-size-to-distance ratio must be equal
q2.opt2: They must be the same actual size
q2.opt3: They must be the same distance away
q2.explain: Angular size depends on the ratio of size to distance — a huge, far object and a small, near one can share the same angular size.

surface_gravity.title: Surface Gravity
surface_gravity.prompt: How strong is the pull of gravity on a planet's surface?
surface_gravity.formula_explainer: Surface gravity depends on both mass and radius — a planet can be more massive than Earth yet have weaker surface gravity if it's also proportionally larger.
surface_gravity.sanity_check: Real value for Earth: 9.8 m/s². Real value for Mars: about 3.7 m/s² — over a third of Earth's, despite Mars having only about 10% of Earth's mass, because Mars is also much smaller.
surface_gravity.challenge_label: Match Mars's real surface gravity: 3.7 m/s²

q1.prompt: Why can a less massive planet sometimes have similar surface gravity to a more massive one?
q1.opt1: Surface gravity depends on radius too — a smaller radius concentrates the same pull closer to the surface
q1.opt2: Mass is the only factor that matters
q1.opt3: Surface gravity is unrelated to mass or radius
q1.explain: Because g = GM/R², a smaller radius increases surface gravity for the same mass — radius matters just as much as mass.

q2.prompt: What would happen to your weight (not mass) if you stood on a planet with half Earth's surface gravity?
q2.opt1: You would weigh half as much
q2.opt3: You would weigh twice as much
q2.explain: Weight is a force proportional to surface gravity — half the gravitational pull means half the weight, even though your actual mass stays the same.

density.title: Density
density.prompt: How tightly packed is a planet's matter, on average?
density.formula_explainer: Density tells you how compact an object's matter is, regardless of its total size — it's a major clue to what a planet is made of.
density.sanity_check: Real value for Earth: about 5.5 g/cm³ (mostly rock and metal). Real value for Saturn: about 0.69 g/cm³ — less dense than water, which is why Saturn would float in a large enough ocean.

q1.prompt: What does a planet's density mainly tell astronomers?
q1.opt1: What the planet is likely made of — rock, metal, gas, or ice
q1.explain: Density is a strong clue to composition: rocky planets like Earth are dense, while gas giants like Saturn are far less dense, dominated by light elements like hydrogen and helium.

q2.prompt: Saturn's density is lower than water's. What would happen if you placed Saturn in a large enough ocean?
q2.opt1: It would float
q2.explain: Saturn's average density (about 0.69 g/cm³) is lower than water's (1 g/cm³), so in principle it would float, given an ocean large enough to hold it.

schwarzschild_radius.title: Schwarzschild Radius
schwarzschild_radius.prompt: How small would an object need to be compressed to become a black hole?
schwarzschild_radius.formula_explainer: The Schwarzschild radius is the size an object's mass would need to be compressed within for its escape velocity to exceed the speed of light — becoming a black hole.
schwarzschild_radius.sanity_check: Real value for the Sun: about 3 km. The Sun isn't a black hole because it's nowhere near that compressed — but if it were, this is how small it would need to be.
schwarzschild_radius.challenge_label: Match the Schwarzschild radius for 10 solar masses: about 30 km

q1.prompt: What does the Schwarzschild radius represent?
q1.opt1: The size an object's mass would need to be compressed within to become a black hole
q1.opt2: The actual physical size of every black hole's core
q1.opt3: The distance a black hole's gravity can be felt
q1.explain: It's a threshold size for a given mass — cross it (get compressed smaller than this radius) and even light can no longer escape.

q2.prompt: Why isn't the Sun a black hole, even though it has a Schwarzschild radius?
q2.opt1: The Sun's actual radius is far larger than its Schwarzschild radius
q2.opt2: The Sun doesn't have enough mass
q2.opt3: Black holes can only form from planets
q2.explain: Every mass has a theoretical Schwarzschild radius, but only becomes a black hole if actually compressed within it — the Sun, at about 696,000 km radius, is nowhere close to its 3 km Schwarzschild radius.

hubble_law.title: Hubble's Law
hubble_law.prompt: How does a galaxy's distance relate to how fast it's moving away from us?
hubble_law.formula_explainer: Hubble's Law describes the expansion of the universe: the farther away a galaxy is, the faster it appears to be moving away from us, in every direction — this is the strongest evidence for cosmic expansion.
hubble_law.sanity_check: This uses a Hubble constant of about 70 km/s per megaparsec — a galaxy 100 million light-years away recedes at roughly 1,500 km/s.
hubble_law.challenge_label: Match a recession velocity of about 4,500 km/s

q1.prompt: What does Hubble's Law tell us about the universe?
q1.opt1: The universe is expanding, with more distant galaxies receding faster
q1.explain: Hubble's Law, discovered by Edwin Hubble in 1929, showed that virtually all distant galaxies are receding from us, and faster ones are farther away — direct evidence the universe is expanding.

q2.prompt: Does Hubble's Law mean we're at the center of the universe?
q2.opt1: No — the same pattern would be seen from any galaxy, since space itself is expanding everywhere
q2.opt2: Yes, this proves Earth is the center
q2.opt3: It only applies to our galaxy specifically
q2.explain: Because space itself is stretching everywhere, an observer in any galaxy would see every other galaxy receding — there's no special center.

parallax.title: Parallax Distance
parallax.prompt: How can astronomers measure a nearby star's distance without ever traveling there?
parallax.formula_explainer: As Earth orbits the Sun, nearby stars appear to shift slightly against distant background stars. Measuring that tiny shift angle directly gives the distance — no assumptions needed, just geometry.
parallax.sanity_check: Real value for Proxima Centauri (the nearest star): parallax of about 0.768 arcseconds gives a distance of about 1.3 parsecs (4.2 light-years).
parallax.challenge_label: Match a distance of 10 parsecs (parallax = 0.1 arcsec)

q1.prompt: What causes the parallax shift used to measure star distances?
q1.opt1: Earth's own orbital motion around the Sun, viewed from opposite sides of the orbit
q1.opt2: The star's own motion through space
q1.explain: Observing a star from opposite points in Earth's orbit (six months apart) gives two different viewing angles, causing the nearby star to appear to shift against the distant background.

q2.prompt: Why is parallax considered one of the most reliable distance measurements in astronomy?
q2.opt1: It relies on direct geometry, not on assumptions about a star's brightness or type
q2.opt2: It only works for extremely distant galaxies
q2.opt3: It requires no telescopes at all
q2.explain: Unlike brightness-based distance methods, which assume things about a star's true luminosity, parallax is pure geometry — making it a foundational, assumption-free technique.

photon_energy.title: Photon Energy
photon_energy.prompt: How much energy does a single particle of light carry?
photon_energy.formula_explainer: Light behaves as both a wave and a stream of particles called photons. Each photon's energy is directly proportional to its frequency — higher-frequency light (like blue or UV) carries more energetic photons than lower-frequency light (like red or infrared).
photon_energy.sanity_check: Real value for green light (~5.5×10¹⁴ Hz): about 3.65×10⁻¹⁹ joules per photon — tiny, but this quantum relationship underlies all of modern physics.
photon_energy.challenge_label: Match the energy of violet light at 7.5×10¹⁴ Hz

q1.prompt: Which carries more energy per photon: red light or blue light?
q1.opt1: Blue light, because it has a higher frequency
q1.opt2: Red light, because it travels faster
q1.opt3: They carry exactly the same energy
q1.explain: Photon energy is proportional to frequency (E = hf), and blue light has a higher frequency than red light, so each blue photon carries more energy.

q2.prompt: This formula, E = hf, was central to which major shift in physics?
q2.opt1: The birth of quantum mechanics
q2.explain: Max Planck and Albert Einstein's work on this exact relationship, showing light's energy comes in discrete packets, helped launch quantum mechanics in the early 20th century.

synodic_period.title: Synodic Period
synodic_period.prompt: How often does a planet appear at the same position relative to Earth and the Sun?
synodic_period.formula_explainer: Because Earth and another planet both orbit the Sun at different speeds, the time between similar alignments (like repeated oppositions) isn't the same as either planet's own year — it's a combination of both.
synodic_period.sanity_check: Real value for Mars: Earth takes 1 year, Mars takes about 1.88 years, giving a synodic period of about 2.135 years — matching the real ~26-month gap between Mars oppositions.
synodic_period.challenge_label: Match Mars's real synodic period: about 2.135 years

q1.prompt: Why isn't a planet's synodic period the same as its actual orbital period?
q1.opt1: Because Earth is also moving, so the alignment depends on both planets' relative motion
q1.opt2: Synodic period and orbital period are always identical
q1.opt3: Synodic period only applies to moons, not planets
q1.explain: The synodic period accounts for Earth's own motion — since we're observing from a moving platform, the apparent repeat interval differs from either planet's actual year.

q2.prompt: What real-world event does Mars's synodic period explain the timing of?
q2.opt1: Why Mars oppositions (best viewing times) happen roughly every 26 months
q2.explain: Mars's synodic period of about 2.135 years (~26 months) is exactly why the best times to view Mars from Earth recur on that same cycle.

rocket_equation.title: The Rocket Equation
rocket_equation.prompt: How much speed can a rocket actually gain from its engines and fuel?
rocket_equation.formula_explainer: Derived by Konstantin Tsiolkovsky in 1903, this equation shows a rocket's total possible speed change depends on how fast it can expel exhaust and what fraction of its total mass is fuel — explaining why multi-stage rockets exist.
rocket_equation.sanity_check: Real value: a rocket with 3 km/s exhaust velocity and a mass ratio of 10 gains about 6.9 km/s — this is why reaching orbit (needing ~9.4 km/s) requires multiple stages.
rocket_equation.challenge_label: Match a Δv of about 6.9 km/s (exhaust 3 km/s, ratio 10)

q1.prompt: Why do most orbital rockets use multiple stages instead of one big one?
q1.opt1: Dropping empty stages reduces mass, letting the rocket equation deliver more total Δv
q1.opt2: Multiple stages are simply a tradition with no real benefit
q1.opt3: A single stage could never physically launch anything
q1.explain: Since the rocket equation depends on the mass ratio at each point, jettisoning empty fuel tanks and engines mid-flight — dropping dead weight — lets each remaining stage do less work, achieving a higher total Δv than one giant stage could alone.

q2.prompt: Who derived the rocket equation that's still used today?
q2.opt1: Konstantin Tsiolkovsky
q2.explain: Russian scientist Konstantin Tsiolkovsky derived this equation in 1903, laying essential groundwork for the entire field of rocketry decades before actual spaceflight was possible.

universe_explorer.title: Universe Explorer
universe_explorer.subtitle: The universe is mostly empty space — filled with a few kinds of extraordinary things.
universe_explorer.scale_instruction: Drag the slider to zoom out — from a planet to the edge of what we can observe.

galaxies.name: Galaxies
galaxies.description: A galaxy is a vast, gravity-bound collection of billions of stars, gas, dust, and dark matter. Our own galaxy, the Milky Way, is a barred spiral holding an estimated 100–400 billion stars — and it's just one of roughly two trillion galaxies in the observable universe.
galaxies.detail: Galaxies themselves cluster together under gravity, forming groups and vast superclusters. The Milky Way belongs to a modest cluster called the Local Group, alongside Andromeda and about 80 smaller galaxies.

nebulae.name: Nebulae
nebulae.description: A nebula is a cloud of gas and dust in space. Some, like the Orion Nebula, are stellar nurseries where gravity slowly pulls material together to form new stars. Others are the glowing remains left behind after a star dies.
nebulae.detail: The famous 'Pillars of Creation' in the Eagle Nebula are columns of gas and dust several light-years tall, where new stars are actively being born inside dense knots of material.

black_holes.name: Black Holes
black_holes.description: A black hole is a region where gravity is so strong that nothing — not even light — can escape once it crosses the event horizon. They form when massive stars collapse. Supermassive versions, millions of times the Sun's mass, sit at the centers of most galaxies, including our own (Sagittarius A*).
black_holes.detail: Black holes can't be observed directly — astronomers detect them by watching how nearby matter behaves, such as stars orbiting an invisible point, or gas heating up and glowing as it spirals in.

stars.name: Stars
stars.description: A star is a massive ball of plasma held together by its own gravity, generating light and heat by fusing hydrogen into helium at its core. Our Sun is a fairly average star — one of hundreds of billions in the Milky Way alone.
stars.detail: A star spends most of its life in a stable phase called the 'main sequence,' fusing hydrogen into helium. The more massive a star is, the hotter it burns — and the shorter its life is.

supernovae.name: Supernovae
supernovae.description: A supernova is the explosive death of a massive star, briefly outshining its entire host galaxy. These explosions forge and scatter heavy elements — like the iron in your blood and the calcium in your bones — throughout the universe.
supernovae.detail: There are two main types: massive stars collapsing under their own gravity, and white dwarfs in binary systems that reach a critical mass and detonate. The second type is so consistent in brightness that astronomers use it to measure cosmic distances.

star_clusters.name: Star Clusters
star_clusters.description: Stars often form and travel in groups. Open clusters, like the Pleiades, are young and loosely bound, with a few hundred stars. Globular clusters are far older and denser, tightly packing tens of thousands to millions of stars into a compact sphere.
star_clusters.detail: Because all the stars in a cluster formed from the same cloud at roughly the same time, clusters are natural laboratories for studying how stars of different masses age differently.

cmb.name: Cosmic Microwave Background
cmb.description: Faint radiation left over from about 380,000 years after the Big Bang, when the universe first became transparent to light. Discovered by accident in 1965, it fills all of space at a nearly uniform temperature of about 2.7 K.
cmb.detail: Tiny temperature variations in the CMB — differences of only about 1 part in 100,000 — mark the seeds of all future structure: regions slightly denser than average eventually grew into today's galaxies.

dark_matter.name: Dark Matter & Dark Energy
dark_matter.description: Roughly 95% of the universe isn't made of the atoms we know. Dark matter, inferred from its gravitational pull on galaxies, makes up about 27%. Dark energy, which drives the universe's accelerating expansion, makes up roughly 68%. Both remain among astronomy's biggest open questions.
dark_matter.detail: Dark matter was first inferred in the 1930s when galaxy clusters appeared to move too fast to stay bound by only their visible mass. Dark energy was only discovered in 1998, from distant supernovae showing the universe's expansion is speeding up.

solar_system.name: The Solar System
solar_system.description: Our home system formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a collapsing cloud of gas and dust. It holds the Sun, 8 planets, over 200 moons, the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, and the icy Kuiper Belt beyond Neptune.
solar_system.detail: The four inner planets are small and rocky; the four outer are much larger gas or ice giants. This split happened because the inner solar system was too hot for ice to survive during formation.

comets.name: Comets
comets.description: Comets are icy leftovers from the outer solar system's formation. As they near the Sun, ice on their surface vaporizes, creating a glowing coma and a tail that always points away from the Sun. Halley's Comet, the most famous, returns roughly every 76 years.
comets.detail: Most comets come from two reservoirs: the Kuiper Belt just beyond Neptune, source of shorter-period comets like Halley's, and the far more distant Oort Cloud, thought to send in comets that take thousands of years to return.

habitable_zone.name: The Habitable Zone
habitable_zone.description: Often called the 'Goldilocks zone,' this is the range of distances from a star where a planet could be warm enough for liquid water but not so hot that it boils away. Earth sits comfortably inside the Sun's habitable zone.
habitable_zone.detail: The habitable zone isn't a guarantee of life — a planet also needs the right atmosphere and geology. A planet can have liquid water outside the zone too, if internal heating keeps water liquid beneath a frozen surface, as on some icy moons.

andromeda.name: The Andromeda Galaxy
andromeda.description: The nearest large galaxy to our own, about 2.5 million light-years away, and visible to the naked eye as a faint smudge on a dark night. It's a spiral galaxy like the Milky Way, and the two are on a slow collision course, expected to merge in roughly 4.5 billion years.
andromeda.detail: Despite being visible to the naked eye, Andromeda's light left it about 2.5 million years ago. It's actually larger in the sky than the full Moon, but too faint and spread out to notice without long-exposure photography.

quasars.name: Quasars
quasars.description: A quasar is the extremely luminous core of a distant galaxy, powered by a supermassive black hole actively feeding on infalling gas and dust. Some quasars outshine their entire host galaxy combined.
quasars.detail: Quasars are among the most distant objects we can observe, meaning their light left them billions of years ago — studying them shows us what the early universe looked like, when galaxies and black holes were still young and voraciously growing.

pulsars.name: Pulsars
pulsars.description: A pulsar is a rapidly rotating neutron star that emits beams of radiation from its magnetic poles. As it spins, the beam sweeps past Earth like a lighthouse, appearing to 'pulse' with extreme regularity.
pulsars.detail: Pulsars were first discovered in 1967 by Jocelyn Bell Burnell, who noticed an unusually precise, repeating radio signal. Some pulsars spin hundreds of times per second and are so regular that astronomers use them as natural cosmic clocks.

brown_dwarfs.name: Brown Dwarfs
brown_dwarfs.description: A brown dwarf is sometimes called a 'failed star' — too massive to be a planet, but too small to sustain the full hydrogen fusion that powers true stars.
brown_dwarfs.detail: Brown dwarfs bridge the gap between the most massive gas giant planets and the smallest true stars, glowing faintly from leftover heat rather than active fusion, and gradually cooling over billions of years.

local_group.name: The Local Group
local_group.description: The Local Group is the cluster of roughly 80 galaxies gravitationally bound together, including our own Milky Way and the Andromeda Galaxy, spanning about 10 million light-years.
local_group.detail: The Milky Way and Andromeda are the Local Group's two largest members, and their slow mutual approach — expected to result in a merger in about 4.5 billion years — will eventually reshape the entire group.

big_bang.name: The Big Bang
big_bang.description: The Big Bang marks the beginning of the observable universe's expansion, roughly 13.8 billion years ago — not an explosion in space, but the start of space itself expanding.
big_bang.detail: Evidence for the Big Bang includes the universe's ongoing expansion (discovered by Edwin Hubble in 1929) and the Cosmic Microwave Background — the leftover glow from the early universe, discovered in 1965.

gravitational_waves.name: Gravitational Waves
gravitational_waves.description: Gravitational waves are ripples in spacetime itself, caused by massive accelerating objects like merging black holes or neutron stars.
gravitational_waves.detail: Predicted by Einstein in 1916, gravitational waves weren't directly detected until 2015, when the LIGO observatory measured the ripple from two black holes merging over a billion light-years away — a discovery that earned the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physics.

earth.label: Earth
earth.blurb: Your home planet — and the baseline for everything that follows.

sun.label: The Sun
sun.blurb: About 109 Earths could line up across the Sun's diameter.

solar_system.label: The Solar System
solar_system.blurb: 1 AU (Astronomical Unit) is the Earth–Sun distance: about 150 million km.

nearest_star.label: To the nearest star system
nearest_star.blurb: Even at the speed of light, it would take over 4 years to reach Alpha Centauri.

milky_way.label: The Milky Way
milky_way.blurb: Our entire galaxy — and we're just one star among hundreds of billions in it.

observable_universe.label: The Observable Universe
observable_universe.blurb: The furthest we can possibly see, limited by the age of the universe and the speed of light.

q1.prompt: Which of these forges the heavy elements found throughout the universe, including in living things?
q1.explain: Supernova explosions create and scatter heavy elements across space — many atoms in your own body were forged this way.

q2.prompt: What does the Cosmic Microwave Background tell us about?
q2.opt1: The current temperature of the Sun
q2.opt2: The universe when it was about 380,000 years old
q2.opt3: The location of the nearest black hole
q2.explain: The CMB is leftover radiation from a specific early moment in the universe's history, giving us a direct snapshot of conditions back then.

q3.prompt: Roughly what fraction of the universe is made of the ordinary atoms we're familiar with?
q3.explain: Dark matter (~27%) and dark energy (~68%) together make up about 95% of the universe, leaving only about 5% as ordinary matter.

q4.prompt: How many stars can globular clusters pack into a relatively compact sphere?
q4.explain: Globular clusters are among the densest stellar environments known, tightly binding tens of thousands to millions of stars.

sky_explorer.title: Sky Explorer
sky_explorer.subtitle: What's actually happening above you tonight.

moon.heading: Tonight's Moon
moon.explainer: The Moon doesn't produce its own light — we see it because it reflects sunlight. As it orbits Earth roughly every 29.5 days, the portion we see lit up changes, giving us the cycle of phases.

planets.heading: Planets you can actually see
planets.text: Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn are often bright enough to see without any telescope. A simple way to tell a planet from a star: planets usually shine with a steady light, while stars twinkle — because starlight travels much further and gets disturbed more by our atmosphere.

constellations.heading: A few constellations to start with

ursa_major.name: Ursa Major (the Great Bear)
ursa_major.text: Contains the "Big Dipper," one of the most recognizable star patterns in the northern sky. Its two end stars point almost directly at Polaris, the North Star.
ursa_major.mythology: Callisto, a nymph loved by Zeus, was transformed into a bear by a jealous Hera. Years later, her son Arcas nearly killed her while hunting without recognizing her — so Zeus placed them both in the sky, as Ursa Major and Ursa Minor, to prevent the tragedy.
ursa_major.tricks: Find the seven bright stars forming the 'Big Dipper' — a distinctive bowl-and-handle shape marking the bear's tail and hindquarters. It's one of the most recognizable patterns in the entire northern sky.
ursa_major.season: Circumpolar from most of the Northern Hemisphere, but highest and most prominent during spring evenings.

q1.prompt: What well-known asterism forms part of Ursa Major?
q1.explain: The Big Dipper's seven bright stars form the bear's tail and hindquarters, making it one of the easiest patterns to spot.

q2.prompt: In myth, who was transformed into the bear that became Ursa Major?
q2.opt1: Callisto
q2.explain: Callisto, a nymph loved by Zeus, was turned into a bear by a jealous Hera and later placed in the sky alongside her son.

q3.prompt: The two end stars of the Big Dipper's bowl point toward which star?
q3.explain: Extending a line through the Big Dipper's two 'pointer stars' leads almost directly to Polaris, the North Star.

orion.name: Orion (the Hunter)
orion.text: Easiest to spot by its three-star belt in a straight line. Visible from most of the world, making it one of the best constellations for beginners.
orion.mythology: Orion was a great hunter in Greek mythology who boasted he could kill any animal on Earth. In punishment, a scorpion was sent to sting him — the origin of why Orion and Scorpius sit on opposite sides of the sky, never visible together.
orion.tricks: Look for the three bright stars in a straight, evenly-spaced line forming Orion's belt. Betelgeuse (reddish, upper-left) marks a shoulder, and Rigel (blue-white, lower-right) marks a foot.
orion.season: Best viewed in the Northern Hemisphere winter evenings (December–March); visible from most of the world.

q1.prompt: What is the easiest way to spot Orion?
q1.opt1: Its three-star belt in a straight, evenly-spaced line
q1.explain: Orion's belt — three evenly-spaced bright stars in a row — is one of the most recognizable patterns in the night sky.

q2.prompt: Which reddish star marks one of Orion's shoulders?
q2.opt1: Betelgeuse
q2.explain: Betelgeuse, a red supergiant, marks Orion's upper shoulder and stands out for its distinctly orange-red color.

q3.prompt: Why are Orion and Scorpius never visible in the sky at the same time?
q3.opt1: In myth, the scorpion killed Orion, so the gods placed them on opposite sides of the sky
q3.opt3: Orion only exists in the Southern Hemisphere
q3.explain: The two constellations sit roughly opposite each other along the sky, so as one rises the other sets — matching the myth of their eternal rivalry.

cassiopeia.name: Cassiopeia
cassiopeia.text: Forms a clear "W" or "M" shape depending on the season, and sits roughly opposite the Big Dipper across Polaris.
cassiopeia.mythology: Cassiopeia was a vain queen who boasted her beauty rivaled the sea nymphs. As punishment, Poseidon placed her in the sky, condemned to circle the celestial pole — spending half of each cycle hanging upside-down.
cassiopeia.tricks: Look for five bright stars forming a clear 'W' or 'M' shape, depending on the time of night and season. It sits roughly opposite the Big Dipper, across Polaris.
cassiopeia.season: Circumpolar from most of the Northern Hemisphere, visible year-round, highest during autumn evenings.

q1.prompt: What shape do Cassiopeia's five brightest stars form?
q1.explain: Cassiopeia's five bright stars form a distinctive zigzag, appearing as a 'W' or 'M' depending on its orientation in the sky.

q2.prompt: In myth, why was Cassiopeia placed in the sky as punishment?
q2.opt1: She boasted her beauty rivaled the sea nymphs
q2.opt2: She stole fire from the gods
q2.explain: Cassiopeia's boast angered the sea nymphs (Nereids), leading Poseidon to place her in the sky, condemned to circle the pole.

q3.prompt: Where does Cassiopeia sit relative to the Big Dipper?
q3.opt3: Only visible from the Southern Hemisphere
q3.explain: Cassiopeia and the Big Dipper sit on opposite sides of Polaris, so as one swings low, the other swings high.

ursa_minor.name: Ursa Minor (the Little Bear)
ursa_minor.text: Home to Polaris, the North Star, at the tip of its tail.
ursa_minor.mythology: In Greek myth, Ursa Minor is often linked to the story of Ursa Major: Callisto was transformed into a bear by a jealous Hera, and her son Arcas — nearly about to kill her while hunting — was also turned into a bear by Zeus and placed beside her in the sky to prevent tragedy.
ursa_minor.tricks: Find the Big Dipper first. The two stars at the end of its bowl (Dubhe and Merak) are called the 'pointer stars' — draw an imaginary line through them and extend it about five times that distance. That line lands almost exactly on Polaris, the tip of Ursa Minor's tail.
ursa_minor.season: Circumpolar from most of the Northern Hemisphere — it never sets and is visible year-round.

q1.prompt: What star sits at the tip of Ursa Minor's tail?
q1.explain: Polaris, the North Star, marks the tip of Ursa Minor's tail and sits almost exactly above Earth's North Pole.

q2.prompt: How do you find Polaris using the Big Dipper?
q2.opt1: Follow the two 'pointer stars' at the end of the bowl and extend the line
q2.opt2: Count seven stars to the right of Orion's belt
q2.explain: The two outer stars of the Big Dipper's bowl point almost directly at Polaris when their line is extended about five times their separation.

q3.prompt: Why is Ursa Minor visible year-round from the Northern Hemisphere?
q3.opt1: It's circumpolar — close enough to the celestial pole that it never sets
q3.opt2: It's extremely bright compared to other constellations
q3.explain: Constellations near the celestial pole, like Ursa Minor, are circumpolar from mid-to-high northern latitudes — they simply circle the pole without ever dipping below the horizon.

leo.name: Leo (the Lion)
leo.text: A zodiac constellation shaped like a crouching lion, easy to spot by its backward-question-mark head.
leo.mythology: Leo represents the Nemean Lion, a beast with an impenetrable hide, slain by Hercules as the first of his Twelve Labors — since no weapon could pierce its skin, Hercules had to strangle it with his bare hands.
leo.tricks: Look for the 'Sickle,' an asterism shaped like a backward question mark that forms the lion's head and mane. The bright star Regulus sits at the bottom of the Sickle, marking the lion's heart.
leo.season: Best viewed in the Northern Hemisphere during spring evenings (March–May).

q1.prompt: What asterism forms Leo's head and mane?
q1.explain: The Sickle is a backward-question-mark-shaped pattern of stars forming Leo's head and mane, one of the easiest asterisms to recognize.

q2.prompt: Which bright star marks the lion's heart, at the base of the Sickle?
q2.opt1: Regulus
q2.explain: Regulus, one of the brightest stars in the night sky, sits at the base of the Sickle and marks Leo's heart.

q3.prompt: In mythology, Leo represents which creature defeated by Hercules?
q3.explain: The Nemean Lion had an impenetrable hide, so Hercules had to defeat it by strangulation rather than any weapon — his first of Twelve Labors.

scorpius.name: Scorpius (the Scorpion)
scorpius.text: One of the most recognizable constellations — it genuinely looks like a scorpion, curved tail and all.
scorpius.mythology: In Greek myth, Scorpius is the scorpion sent to kill the boastful hunter Orion. The gods placed them on opposite sides of the sky so the two would never rise at the same time again.
scorpius.tricks: Find the bright red star Antares — its name means 'rival of Mars' for its similar reddish color — marking the scorpion's heart. Follow the curving line of stars from there to the stinger-shaped tail.
scorpius.season: Best viewed in the Northern Hemisphere summer (June–August), low on the southern horizon; appears much higher from the Southern Hemisphere.

q1.prompt: What bright red star marks the scorpion's heart?
q1.explain: Antares — whose name means 'rival of Mars' — is a red supergiant marking Scorpius's heart.

q2.prompt: According to myth, why are Scorpius and Orion never visible in the sky at the same time?
q2.opt1: The gods placed them on opposite sides of the sky after the scorpion killed Orion
q2.opt2: They are the same constellation viewed from different seasons
q2.opt3: Orion is only visible from the Southern Hemisphere
q2.explain: In the myth, the scorpion that killed Orion was placed opposite him in the sky, so as one rises the other sets.

q3.prompt: From which hemisphere does Scorpius appear highest and most prominent?
q3.opt3: It appears equally high from everywhere
q3.explain: Scorpius lies well south of the celestial equator, so it rides low near the horizon in the north but climbs high overhead from southern latitudes.

taurus.name: Taurus (the Bull)
taurus.text: Contains two famous star clusters — the Pleiades and the Hyades — marking the bull's shoulder and face.
taurus.mythology: Taurus represents Zeus disguised as a magnificent white bull, whom he used to carry away the Phoenician princess Europa across the sea to Crete.
taurus.tricks: Find the V-shaped Hyades cluster, forming the bull's face, with the bright orange star Aldebaran marking its eye. The Pleiades cluster sits just beyond, marking the bull's shoulder.
taurus.season: Best viewed in the Northern Hemisphere winter evenings (November–February).

q1.prompt: Which star cluster forms the V-shaped face of the bull?
q1.explain: The Hyades cluster forms the recognizable V-shape of Taurus's face, with Aldebaran marking the eye.

q2.prompt: What famous star cluster sits on the bull's shoulder?
q2.opt1: The Pleiades
q2.explain: The Pleiades, also called the Seven Sisters, is one of the closest and most easily visible star clusters, sitting on Taurus's shoulder.

q3.prompt: In Greek myth, Taurus represents Zeus disguised as what, carrying away Europa?
q3.explain: Zeus transformed into a gentle white bull to approach and carry off the princess Europa, the origin of Taurus.

cygnus.name: Cygnus (the Swan)
cygnus.text: Also called the Northern Cross, appearing to fly along the band of the Milky Way.
cygnus.mythology: Cygnus is linked to several myths, including Zeus transforming into a swan, and the story of Orpheus, the legendary musician, placed among the stars near his lyre after his death.
cygnus.tricks: Look for the bright star Deneb marking the tail, with the constellation forming a distinctive cross shape — the 'Northern Cross' — stretched along the glowing band of the Milky Way.
cygnus.season: Best viewed in the Northern Hemisphere summer and autumn evenings (June–November).

q1.prompt: What common nickname describes Cygnus's cross-like shape?
q1.explain: Cygnus's brightest stars form a distinctive cross shape, widely nicknamed the Northern Cross.

q2.prompt: What bright star marks the swan's tail?
q2.opt1: Deneb
q2.explain: Deneb, one of the brightest stars in the sky, marks the tail of Cygnus.

q3.prompt: Along which feature of the night sky does Cygnus appear to fly?
q3.explain: Cygnus stretches along the bright band of the Milky Way, appearing to fly through our galaxy's disk as seen from Earth.

sagittarius.name: Sagittarius (the Archer)
sagittarius.text: Points toward the very center of our own Milky Way galaxy.
sagittarius.mythology: Usually depicted as a centaur archer, Sagittarius is often identified with Chiron, the wise centaur who taught many Greek heroes, though other myths link it to different archer-centaurs.
sagittarius.tricks: Find the 'Teapot,' an easily recognizable teapot-shaped pattern formed by its brightest stars. The 'steam' rising from its spout points directly toward the dense star clouds marking our galaxy's center.
sagittarius.season: Best viewed in the Northern Hemisphere summer (June–August), low in the southern sky.

q1.prompt: What easily recognizable shape do Sagittarius's brightest stars form?
q1.explain: The brightest stars of Sagittarius form a distinctive teapot shape, one of the most recognizable asterisms in the sky.

q2.prompt: What does the 'steam' from the Teapot's spout point toward?
q2.opt1: The center of the Milky Way galaxy
q2.explain: Looking toward the Teapot's spout points almost directly at the galactic center, where dense star clouds and Sagittarius A* (our galaxy's supermassive black hole) lie.

q3.prompt: Sagittarius is most often depicted as what mythological figure?
q3.explain: Sagittarius is traditionally shown as a centaur — half-human, half-horse — drawing a bow, often linked to the wise centaur Chiron.

q1.prompt: Why does the Moon go through phases?
q1.opt1: Because we see different amounts of its sunlit half as it orbits Earth
q1.opt2: Because Earth's shadow covers it every night
q1.explain: The Moon's phases come from our changing view of the half that's lit by the Sun — the Moon itself doesn't change shape.

q2.prompt: What's a simple way to tell a planet from a star in the night sky?
q2.opt1: Planets are always bigger looking
q2.opt3: Stars are only visible in winter
q2.explain: Starlight twinkles because it travels much farther and gets disturbed more by our atmosphere; planets usually shine with a steadier light.

moon_game.prompt: Before we tell you: which phase do you think the Moon is in tonight?
moon_game.close: Close, but not quite — here's the real one:

planet_game.heading: Planet or Star?
planet_game.prompt: A point of light in the sky shines with a perfectly steady glow, never flickering. Is it a planet or a star?
planet_game.correct: Right! Planets shine steadily because they're close enough that their light isn't disturbed much by our atmosphere.
planet_game.incorrect: Actually, a steady, non-twinkling light is the sign of a planet — try again.

exoplanet_hunter.title: Exoplanet Hunter
exoplanet_hunter.subtitle: Find a planet by watching starlight dim — this is the transit method, and it's how most known exoplanets were discovered.
exoplanet_hunter.instruction: One of these three light curves shows a planet passing in front of its star. Which one?
exoplanet_hunter.correct: Correct — that dip is a transit.
exoplanet_hunter.incorrect: Not quite. Look for a brief, symmetric dip in brightness, then look again.
exoplanet_hunter.explanation: When a planet passes in front of its star from our point of view, it blocks a tiny fraction of the star's light, causing a small, temporary, repeating dip in brightness. This is the transit method — it's how missions like Kepler and TESS have found thousands of exoplanets.

size_challenge.heading: Now estimate the planet's size
size_challenge.instruction: The depth of the dip relates directly to the planet's size compared to its star: depth = (planet radius / star radius)². Adjust the dip depth below and see the size ratio update.

q1.prompt: If a light curve shows a deeper dip, what does that suggest about the planet?
q1.opt2: It's larger relative to its star
q1.explain: Since dip depth = (planet radius / star radius)², a deeper dip directly means a proportionally larger planet relative to its star.

q2.prompt: What space telescope mission discovered thousands of exoplanets using the transit method?
q2.opt1: Kepler
q2.explain: Launched in 2009, Kepler stared continuously at one patch of sky and discovered over 2,700 confirmed exoplanets, mostly via transits.

q3.prompt: Why can the transit method only detect planets whose orbits happen to align edge-on to our view?
q3.opt1: Only then does the planet pass directly in front of the star from our perspective
q3.opt2: Edge-on orbits are more gravitationally stable
q3.opt3: It's simply a limitation of telescope resolution
q3.explain: Transits require the planet's orbital plane to line up so it crosses in front of the star as seen from Earth — many systems are tilted so this never happens, meaning surveys miss most planets around any given star.

radial_velocity.instruction: A planet's gravity tugs its star back and forth slightly as it orbits. This causes the star's own light to shift periodically — astronomers detect this 'wobble' instead of seeing the planet directly. Which curve below shows a real periodic wobble?
radial_velocity.correct: Correct — that's a real periodic wobble.
radial_velocity.incorrect: Not quite. A real wobble repeats in a smooth, regular pattern — look again.
radial_velocity.explanation: This is the radial velocity method: as a planet orbits, its gravity pulls its star into a small orbit of its own, shifting the star's light periodically toward and away from us. It was used to find the first exoplanet ever confirmed around a Sun-like star, in 1995.

q1.prompt: What does the radial velocity method actually detect?
q1.opt1: Periodic shifts in the star's own light caused by the planet's gravity
q1.opt2: A direct photograph of the planet
q1.explain: This method never sees the planet directly — it detects the star's light shifting periodically as the star wobbles under the planet's gravitational pull.

q2.prompt: What was 51 Pegasi b, discovered in 1995 using this method?
q2.opt1: The first confirmed exoplanet orbiting a Sun-like star
q2.opt2: The first exoplanet ever imaged directly
q2.opt3: The closest known exoplanet to Earth
q2.explain: 51 Pegasi b's discovery via radial velocity earned its discoverers the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics.

q3.prompt: What kind of planetary orbit is hardest for the radial velocity method to detect?
q3.opt1: An orbit seen face-on, straight down from above
q3.explain: Radial velocity only detects motion toward or away from us; a face-on orbit produces almost no such motion, making it far harder to detect this way.

habitable_zone.heading: Habitable Zone Calculator
habitable_zone.instruction: The habitable zone is the range of distances from a star where a planet could have liquid water. A simple estimate: habitable distance (AU) ≈ √(star's luminosity ÷ Sun's luminosity).
habitable_zone.verdict_in_zone: Roughly within the habitable zone — worth further investigation.
habitable_zone.verdict_out_zone: Likely outside the habitable zone at this simple estimate.

q1.prompt: A star has 4× the Sun's luminosity. Roughly how far out does its habitable zone sit?
q1.explain: Habitable distance ≈ √(L/L☉) = √4 = 2 AU — a more luminous star pushes its habitable zone farther out.

q2.prompt: What is the 'runaway greenhouse effect,' and which planet suffers from it?
q2.opt1: Trapped heat boiling away all surface water, as happened to Venus
q2.opt2: A planet losing its atmosphere entirely, as happened to Mars
q2.opt3: A planet freezing solid, as happened to Pluto
q2.explain: Venus, though only slightly closer to the Sun than Earth, suffered a runaway greenhouse effect: trapped heat boiled away its oceans and left a scorching, toxic atmosphere.

q3.prompt: Why do scientists define both a 'conservative' and an 'optimistic' habitable zone instead of just one boundary?
q3.opt1: Because the exact edges depend on assumptions about atmosphere and geology that aren't fully certain
q3.opt2: Because they can't agree on how far the Sun's habitable zone extends
q3.opt3: Because every planet has a different distance to its star
q3.explain: Where liquid water can survive depends on a planet's specific atmosphere and geology, which we usually can't observe directly — so scientists give a range rather than one precise line.

extra_concepts.heading: Two things this simple calculator doesn't capture
extra_concepts.conservative_optimistic: Scientists actually define a 'conservative' zone (where Earth-like conditions are most likely) and a wider 'optimistic' zone (where liquid water is possible under some conditions) — this calculator shows a simplified single estimate between the two.
extra_concepts.runaway_greenhouse: Too close to a star, a planet can suffer a 'runaway greenhouse effect' — like what happened to Venus — where heat gets trapped so effectively that any surface water boils away entirely, even before reaching the calculated inner edge.

asteroid_hunter.title: Asteroid Hunter
asteroid_hunter.subtitle: Spot the object that moved — this is how astronomers really find asteroids.
asteroid_hunter.instruction: These two star fields were captured a short time apart. Stars stay fixed — but one object moved. Click it in Frame 2.
asteroid_hunter.frame2_label: Frame 2 — click the object that moved
asteroid_hunter.correct: Found it. That's how a moving object gives itself away against a fixed background of stars.
asteroid_hunter.incorrect: Not that one — look for the dot that's in a different position between the two frames.
asteroid_hunter.explanation: Real astronomers use this exact technique, called "blink comparison": they compare images of the same patch of sky taken minutes or hours apart. Stars are so far away they appear fixed, but a nearby asteroid visibly shifts position — that's the giveaway.
asteroid_hunter.simulated_label: Simulated for learning purposes — not a real sky image

q1.prompt: Why does an asteroid appear to move between two images of the same sky patch, while stars don't?
q1.opt1: Asteroids are much closer to Earth than stars are
q1.opt3: Stars are too small to photograph
q1.explain: Because asteroids are relatively close, their position against the fixed background of much more distant stars visibly shifts over time — this is the basis of the blink comparison method.

q2.prompt: Who is generally credited with using the blink comparator technique to discover Pluto in 1930?
q2.opt1: Clyde Tombaugh
q2.explain: Tombaugh used a blink comparator device to compare photographic plates and spotted Pluto by its shift against the fixed background stars.

q3.prompt: Besides asteroids, what other kind of object can blink comparison also help detect?
q3.opt1: Comets and other small moving solar system bodies
q3.explain: Any relatively nearby object that shifts position between exposures — comets, asteroids, even fast-moving satellites — can be revealed this way.

classify.instruction: Real asteroids are grouped by their distance from the Sun. Given the distance below, classify this asteroid.
classify.incorrect: Not quite — check the ranges below and try again.
classify.explainer: Near-Earth Objects (NEOs) come within about 1.3 AU of the Sun and are tracked closely for impact risk. Most asteroids orbit in the Main Belt between Mars and Jupiter (roughly 2.1–3.3 AU). Jupiter Trojans share Jupiter's orbit (about 5.2 AU), clustered 60° ahead of or behind the planet.

q1.prompt: Most known asteroids in our solar system orbit in which region?
q1.opt1: The Main Belt, between Mars and Jupiter
q1.explain: The Main Belt between Mars and Jupiter (roughly 2.1–3.3 AU) holds the vast majority of known asteroids in the solar system.

q2.prompt: Why are Near-Earth Objects (NEOs) tracked so closely by astronomers?
q2.opt1: Their orbits bring them close enough to Earth to pose a potential impact risk
q2.explain: NEOs' orbits cross close to Earth's, so agencies like NASA's Center for Near-Earth Object Studies track them closely to assess any long-term impact risk.

q3.prompt: Jupiter Trojans share Jupiter's orbit. Where exactly do they cluster?
q3.opt1: About 60° ahead of or behind Jupiter, at gravitationally stable points
q3.opt2: Directly behind Jupiter, touching its atmosphere
q3.opt3: Scattered randomly all along Jupiter's orbit
q3.explain: Trojans cluster near the Lagrange points L4 and L5, roughly 60° ahead of and behind Jupiter, where the combined gravity of the Sun and Jupiter creates stable zones.

rotation.instruction: Asteroids are irregularly shaped, so as they spin, the sunlight they reflect toward us rises and falls. Read this brightness curve and estimate the rotation period.
rotation.correct: Correct — that's the repeating pattern's period.
rotation.incorrect: Not quite — look for how long it takes the pattern to repeat one full cycle, then try again.
rotation.explainer: This technique, called lightcurve photometry, is one of the main real ways astronomers measure how fast an asteroid spins — and irregular shapes are exactly why the brightness isn't constant.

q1.prompt: Why does an asteroid's brightness typically rise and fall twice per full rotation?
q1.opt1: Because it's irregularly shaped, showing a longer and a shorter face to us once each per spin
q1.opt2: Because it passes behind the Sun twice
q1.opt3: Because it changes color as it spins
q1.explain: Most asteroids are not spherical — as an elongated shape rotates, it presents more or less reflective surface area to us twice per full spin, creating two brightness peaks and two dips.

q2.prompt: What shape of asteroid produces the strongest brightness variation as it rotates?
q2.opt1: A highly elongated, irregular shape
q2.opt3: A flat disk facing us directly
q2.explain: A perfectly spherical asteroid shows almost no brightness change no matter how fast it spins, since it always presents the same silhouette; elongated shapes show the biggest swings.

q3.prompt: What limits how fast a loosely-bound 'rubble pile' asteroid can spin?
q3.opt1: Beyond a critical speed, centrifugal force would fling loose material off
q3.opt2: There's no physical limit at all
q3.opt3: Asteroids slow down the moment they form
q3.explain: This is the real 'spin barrier' — most rubble-pile asteroids don't spin faster than about once every 2.2 hours, because faster rotation would overcome their weak self-gravity and fling material off.

stellar_detective.title: Stellar Detective
stellar_detective.subtitle: A star's color is a direct readout of its surface temperature.
stellar_detective.question: Based on this temperature, what spectral class is this star?
stellar_detective.incorrect: Not quite — check the temperature ranges below and try again.
stellar_detective.explainer: Astronomers classify stars into spectral types — O, B, A, F, G, K, M, from hottest to coolest — based on temperature, which also determines color. Hotter stars glow blue-white; cooler stars glow orange-red. Our Sun is a G-type star, at around 5,778 K.

q1.prompt: Which spectral class is our Sun?
q1.explain: The Sun is a G-type star, with a surface temperature of about 5,778 K — putting it right in the yellow part of the spectrum.

q2.prompt: White dwarfs are extremely hot but not very luminous. What must be true of their radius?
q2.opt1: It must be very small, since luminosity depends on radius squared as well as temperature to the 4th power
q2.opt3: Radius doesn't affect this at all
q2.explain: Since luminosity depends on both R² and T⁴, a hot-but-dim star must have a tiny radius — white dwarfs are roughly Earth-sized despite being hotter than the Sun.

q3.prompt: Which spectral class contains the coolest, reddest stars, including most red dwarfs?
q3.explain: M-type stars, under about 3,700 K, are the coolest and reddest class — and also by far the most common type of star in the galaxy.

glossary.title: Astronomy Glossary
glossary.subtitle: Every term used across Astralis, explained simply, in one place.

au.name: AU (Astronomical Unit)
au.def: The average distance from Earth to the Sun — about 150 million km. Used to measure distances within a solar system.

light_year.name: Light-year
light_year.def: The distance light travels in one year — about 9.46 trillion km. Used to measure distances between stars and galaxies.

parsec.name: Parsec
parsec.def: A distance unit equal to about 3.26 light-years, based on how much a star's position appears to shift (parallax) as Earth orbits the Sun.

escape_velocity.name: Escape Velocity
escape_velocity.def: The minimum speed an object needs to permanently break free from a body's gravity without further propulsion.

orbital_velocity.name: Orbital Velocity
orbital_velocity.def: The speed an object needs to maintain a stable orbit around a body, balancing gravity's pull against its own motion.

transit_method.name: Transit Method
transit_method.def: A way of detecting exoplanets by observing the tiny, periodic dip in a star's brightness as a planet passes in front of it.

radial_velocity.name: Radial Velocity Method
radial_velocity.def: A way of detecting exoplanets by observing the periodic 'wobble' a planet's gravity causes in its star's light.

habitable_zone.name: Habitable Zone
habitable_zone.def: The range of distances from a star where a planet could be warm enough for liquid water, but not so hot that it boils away.

spectral_class.name: Spectral Class
spectral_class.def: A classification system for stars (O, B, A, F, G, K, M — hottest to coolest) based on surface temperature and color.

luminosity.name: Luminosity
luminosity.def: The total energy a star radiates per second — its true brightness, independent of how far away it is.

apparent_brightness.name: Apparent Brightness
apparent_brightness.def: How bright a star looks from Earth, which depends on both its true luminosity and its distance from us.

aphelion_perihelion.name: Aphelion / Perihelion
aphelion_perihelion.def: The farthest point (aphelion) and nearest point (perihelion) in an object's orbit around the Sun.

apogee_perigee.name: Apogee / Perigee
apogee_perigee.def: The farthest point (apogee) and nearest point (perigee) in an object's orbit around Earth.

blackbody_radiation.name: Blackbody Radiation
blackbody_radiation.def: The characteristic glow any object emits based purely on its temperature — hotter objects glow bluer, cooler ones redder.

event_horizon.name: Event Horizon
event_horizon.def: The boundary around a black hole beyond which nothing, not even light, can escape its gravity.

supernova.name: Supernova
supernova.def: The explosive death of a massive star, or of a white dwarf that reaches a critical mass — briefly outshining an entire galaxy.

nebula.name: Nebula
nebula.def: A cloud of gas and dust in space — sometimes a nursery where new stars form, sometimes the remains left behind after a star dies.

globular_cluster.name: Globular Cluster
globular_cluster.def: A dense, roughly spherical group of tens of thousands to millions of old stars, tightly bound by gravity.

neo.name: NEO (Near-Earth Object)
neo.def: An asteroid or comet whose orbit brings it close enough to Earth's to be tracked for potential impact risk.

trojan_asteroid.name: Trojan Asteroid
trojan_asteroid.def: An asteroid sharing a planet's orbit, clustered near gravitationally stable points about 60° ahead of or behind it.

lightcurve.name: Lightcurve
lightcurve.def: A graph of an object's brightness over time — used to study asteroid rotation, exoplanet transits, and more.

synodic_month.name: Synodic Month
synodic_month.def: The time it takes the Moon to return to the same phase (e.g. full moon to full moon) — about 29.5 days.

keplers_third_law.name: Kepler's Third Law
keplers_third_law.def: The mathematical relationship between a planet's orbital period and its distance from the Sun: the period squared is proportional to the distance cubed.

redshift.name: Redshift
redshift.def: The stretching of light to longer, redder wavelengths as an object moves away from us or as space itself expands.

orbital_period.name: Orbital Period
orbital_period.def: The time an object takes to complete one full orbit around another body — Earth's orbital period around the Sun is one year.

rotation_period.name: Rotation Period
rotation_period.def: The time an object takes to spin once on its own axis — Earth's rotation period is about 24 hours, defining a day.

circumpolar.name: Circumpolar
circumpolar.def: A star or constellation that never sets below the horizon from a given location, instead circling the celestial pole endlessly.

asterism.name: Asterism
asterism.def: A recognizable star pattern that isn't itself an official constellation, like the Big Dipper (part of Ursa Major) or the Summer Triangle.

zodiac.name: Zodiac
zodiac.def: The band of 12 (traditionally) constellations that the Sun appears to pass through over the course of a year, as seen from Earth.

main_belt.name: Main Belt
main_belt.def: The region between Mars and Jupiter (roughly 2.1–3.3 AU from the Sun) where most known asteroids in the solar system orbit.

lagrange_point.name: Lagrange Point
lagrange_point.def: A location in space where the gravity of two large bodies balances the motion of a smaller object, letting it stay in a stable relative position.

blink_comparator.name: Blink Comparator
blink_comparator.def: A device (and technique) astronomers use to rapidly compare two images of the same sky, revealing any object that moved between them.

white_dwarf.name: White Dwarf
white_dwarf.def: The hot, extremely dense, Earth-sized remnant left behind after a Sun-like star exhausts its fuel and sheds its outer layers.

red_giant.name: Red Giant
red_giant.def: A late-life stage of a star like the Sun, where it swells enormously and cools, glowing red, after exhausting hydrogen fuel in its core.

neutron_star.name: Neutron Star
neutron_star.def: An extremely dense stellar remnant left after a massive star's core collapses in a supernova, packing more mass than the Sun into a city-sized sphere.

main_sequence.name: Main Sequence
main_sequence.def: The stable, long-lasting phase of a star's life when it fuses hydrogen into helium in its core — most stars, including the Sun, are in this phase.

cosmic_microwave_background.name: Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB)
cosmic_microwave_background.def: Faint radiation left over from about 380,000 years after the Big Bang, filling all of space at a nearly uniform temperature of 2.7 K.

dark_matter.name: Dark Matter
dark_matter.def: An invisible form of matter, detected only through its gravitational effects, that makes up roughly 27% of the universe.

dark_energy.name: Dark Energy
dark_energy.def: A mysterious force driving the accelerating expansion of the universe, making up roughly 68% of its total energy content.

observable_universe.name: Observable Universe
observable_universe.def: The portion of the universe we can possibly see, limited by the age of the universe and the speed of light — about 93 billion light-years across.

solar_system.name: Solar System
solar_system.def: The Sun and everything gravitationally bound to it — planets, moons, asteroids, comets — formed together about 4.6 billion years ago.

kuiper_belt.name: Kuiper Belt
kuiper_belt.def: A region beyond Neptune's orbit filled with icy bodies, including Pluto, and the source of many shorter-period comets.

oort_cloud.name: Oort Cloud
oort_cloud.def: A vast, distant, spherical shell of icy objects surrounding the solar system, thought to be the source of long-period comets.

wien_law.name: Wien's Law
wien_law.def: A rule stating that the wavelength at which an object radiates most strongly is inversely proportional to its temperature — hotter objects glow bluer.

stefan_boltzmann_law.name: Stefan–Boltzmann Law
stefan_boltzmann_law.def: A rule stating that a star's luminosity depends on both its surface area and temperature: L ∝ R²T⁴.

inverse_square_law.name: Inverse-Square Law
inverse_square_law.def: A rule stating that a light source's apparent brightness falls off with the square of the distance from it.

schwarzschild_radius.name: (Related) Photon Energy
schwarzschild_radius.def: The energy carried by a single photon of light, given by E = hf, where h is Planck's constant and f is the light's frequency — a foundational idea in quantum physics.

circumstellar_habitable_zone.name: Conservative vs. Optimistic Habitable Zone
circumstellar_habitable_zone.def: Two boundary estimates for where liquid water could exist: a narrower 'conservative' zone considered most likely, and a wider 'optimistic' one possible under some conditions.

runaway_greenhouse.name: Runaway Greenhouse Effect
runaway_greenhouse.def: A process where a planet traps heat so effectively that any surface water boils away entirely — this happened to Venus.

gravitational_lensing.name: Gravitational Lensing
gravitational_lensing.def: The bending of light around a massive object, like a galaxy cluster, which can magnify or distort the image of objects behind it.

declination_right_ascension.name: Declination & Right Ascension
declination_right_ascension.def: The two coordinates astronomers use to pinpoint an object's fixed position in the sky, similar to latitude and longitude on Earth.

zenith.name: Zenith
zenith.def: The point in the sky directly overhead an observer, at 90° above the horizon.

occultation.name: Occultation
occultation.def: An event where one astronomical object passes directly in front of another, temporarily blocking it from view — for example, the Moon occulting a star.

conjunction.name: Conjunction
conjunction.def: An event where two astronomical objects appear very close together in the sky, as seen from Earth.

meteor_meteorite.name: Meteor vs. Meteorite
meteor_meteorite.def: A meteor is the streak of light from a small object burning up in Earth's atmosphere; a meteorite is a piece of that object that survives to reach the ground.

albedo.name: Albedo
albedo.def: A measure of how much light a surface reflects, from 0 (absorbs everything) to 1 (reflects everything) — snow has a high albedo, dark rock a low one.
