cosmic_comedy.title: ബഹിരാകാശ തമാശ
cosmic_comedy.subtitle: ശരിക്കും ചിരിപ്പിക്കുന്ന തമാശകളിലൂടെ യഥാർത്ഥ ജ്യോതിശാസ്ത്രം പഠിക്കുക.
cosmic_comedy.hint: പച്ച ഡോട്ട് = പഠിച്ചവ. ചാടാൻ ഏതെങ്കിലും ഡോട്ട് ടാപ്പ് ചെയ്യുക.

black_hole_party.setup: Why don’t black holes ever throw parties?
black_hole_party.punchline: Because no one who goes in ever comes out — and the snacks can’t escape either.
black_hole_party.science: A black hole’s gravity is so strong that not even light can escape past a boundary called the event horizon. That’s why they look “black”.

light_year_beer.setup: A light-year is the distance light travels in one year. So if a spaceship goes at light speed for a year…
light_year_beer.punchline: …it still won’t get you a free drink. A light-year is a distance, not a time — and bars don’t take astronomical units.
light_year_beer.science: A light-year is about 9.5 trillion kilometres. It’s a unit of distance, not time. People often mix this up!

astronaut_space.setup: Why did the astronaut break up with their partner?
astronaut_space.science: Jokes aside, “space” in astronomy means the nearly empty regions between planets, stars and galaxies — mostly vacuum with tiny amounts of gas and dust.

saturn_rings.setup: Why is Saturn so good at keeping secrets?
saturn_rings.punchline: It has a lot of rings — but none of them are phone rings you can answer.
saturn_rings.science: Saturn’s rings are made of countless chunks of ice and rock, from tiny grains to house-sized pieces, orbiting the planet.

moon_cow.setup: How do you know the Moon is friendly?
moon_cow.punchline: It always comes out at night to keep Earth company — and it never asks for rent.
moon_cow.science: The Moon is tidally locked: we always see roughly the same face. It reflects sunlight, which is why it shines at night.

sun_glasses.setup: Why does the Sun never need glasses?
sun_glasses.punchline: Because it’s already a star with perfect vision — it sees everything in a new light every 8 minutes.
sun_glasses.science: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach Earth. The Sun is an ordinary star, just much closer than the others.

comet_ice.setup: What do you call a comet that tells jokes?
comet_ice.punchline: A “pun-damental” snowball — dirty ice with a glowing sense of humour.
comet_ice.science: Comets are icy bodies. When they near the Sun, ice turns to gas and releases dust, forming the bright coma and tail we see.

galaxy_bar.setup: Why did the galaxy go to the bar?
galaxy_bar.punchline: It heard the drinks were on the house — and the house was 100,000 light-years wide.
galaxy_bar.science: Our Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy roughly 100,000 light-years across and contains hundreds of billions of stars.

neutron_diet.setup: Why are neutron stars terrible at dieting?
neutron_diet.punchline: They already packed a whole star’s mass into a city-sized ball — there’s nowhere left to shrink.
neutron_diet.science: A neutron star is the crushed core of a massive star after a supernova. A teaspoon of its material would weigh billions of tonnes on Earth.

telescope_far.setup: Why did the telescope break up with the microscope?
telescope_far.punchline: It said, “You’re too focused on the small stuff. I need to see other stars.”
telescope_far.science: Telescopes collect light from distant objects. Bigger mirrors or lenses gather more light, letting us see fainter and farther things.

orbit_commitment.setup: Why are planets so committed to the Sun?
orbit_commitment.punchline: They’re stuck in a long-term orbit — divorce would require escaping the entire solar system.
orbit_commitment.science: An orbit is a balance between gravity pulling inward and the planet’s sideways speed. Change either too much and the path changes.

big_bang_noise.setup: What did the universe say after the Big Bang?
big_bang_noise.science: The Big Bang wasn’t an explosion in space — it was the rapid expansion of space itself. The universe has been expanding ever since.

mars_single.punchline: It has a lot of red flags — literally. The whole planet is covered in rusty dust.
mars_single.science: Mars looks red because its surface is rich in iron oxide (rust). It’s colder and much thinner-aired than Earth.

constellation_connect.setup: Why are constellation maps so popular with kids?
constellation_connect.punchline: They’re the original connect-the-dots — except the dots are nuclear furnaces trillions of kilometres away.
constellation_connect.science: Constellations are patterns humans imagined by connecting stars as seen from Earth. The stars in one constellation are usually not close to each other in space.

eclipse_shadow.setup: Why did the Moon cover the Sun during the meeting?
eclipse_shadow.punchline: It wanted to throw some shade — scientifically speaking.
eclipse_shadow.science: A solar eclipse happens when the Moon passes between Earth and the Sun and casts a shadow on Earth. A lunar eclipse is when Earth shadows the Moon.

asteroid_belt.setup: Why did the asteroid apply for a job in fashion?
asteroid_belt.punchline: It wanted to work the belt — the one between Mars and Jupiter.
asteroid_belt.science: Most asteroids in our solar system orbit in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. They’re leftover rocky pieces from the solar system’s formation.

vacuum_clean.punchline: No — it’s a vacuum. Cleaning is included, but oxygen is not.
vacuum_clean.science: Space is an extremely good vacuum compared with Earth’s air, but it’s not perfectly empty. There’s sparse gas, dust, radiation and magnetic fields.

redshift_blues.setup: Why was the distant galaxy feeling blue?
redshift_blues.punchline: It wasn’t — from Earth it looked redshifted. The universe stretched its light on the way here.
redshift_blues.science: As space expands, light from far galaxies stretches to longer (redder) wavelengths. This redshift tells us the universe is expanding.

pulsar_clock.setup: Why do astronomers trust pulsars with the time?
pulsar_clock.punchline: They’re the universe’s most reliable spinning lighthouses — tick, tick, tick, for millions of years.
pulsar_clock.science: Pulsars are rotating neutron stars that sweep radio beams past Earth like lighthouse beams. Their pulses are extremely regular.

exoplanet_house.setup: Why did the exoplanet refuse to move in with its star?
exoplanet_house.punchline: The neighbourhood was too hot — it preferred a house in the habitable zone.
exoplanet_house.science: An exoplanet is a planet orbiting a star other than the Sun. The “habitable zone” is the distance range where liquid water could exist on a rocky world.

milky_way_spill.setup: Who spilled milk across the night sky?
milky_way_spill.punchline: Nobody — that’s our galaxy seen from the inside, a river of countless distant suns.
milky_way_spill.science: The Milky Way band is the combined glow of stars in our galactic disk. We see it edge-on because we live inside that disk.

gravity_pull.setup: Why is gravity such a great friend?
gravity_pull.punchline: It always brings you back down to Earth — whether you like it or not.
gravity_pull.science: Gravity is the attraction between masses. On Earth it gives us weight; in space it keeps moons and planets in orbit.

supernova_exit.setup: How does a massive star leave a party?
supernova_exit.punchline: It goes out with a bang — a supernova that can outshine an entire galaxy for weeks.
supernova_exit.science: A supernova is the explosive death of a massive star. It seeds the galaxy with heavy elements that later form new stars and planets.

dark_matter_room.setup: Why is dark matter so hard to invite to dinner?
dark_matter_room.punchline: It doesn’t show up on any photos — it only reveals itself by how it pulls on the guests who do.
dark_matter_room.science: Dark matter doesn’t emit or absorb light, so we can’t see it directly. We detect it by its gravitational effect on stars and galaxies.

habitable_zone_rent.setup: Why are planets in the habitable zone always stressed about rent?
habitable_zone_rent.punchline: Too close to the star and you burn; too far and you freeze. Location is everything.
habitable_zone_rent.science: The habitable zone is the orbital range around a star where a rocky planet could have liquid water. It’s sometimes called the Goldilocks zone — not too hot, not too cold.

jupiter_weight.setup: Why shouldn’t you try to stand on Jupiter?
jupiter_weight.punchline: There’s no solid ground — and you’d weigh enough to make a bathroom scale quit its job.
jupiter_weight.science: Jupiter is a gas giant. It has no solid surface like Earth’s. Under the clouds, pressure and temperature rise until hydrogen behaves like a liquid metal.

venus_day.setup: Why is a day on Venus longer than its year?
venus_day.punchline: Venus spins so slowly that it finishes one trip around the Sun before it finishes one spin. Talk about taking your time getting dressed.
venus_day.science: Venus takes about 243 Earth days to rotate once, but only about 225 Earth days to orbit the Sun — so its day is longer than its year.

mercury_hot.setup: Why does Mercury never need a winter coat or sunscreen at the same time?
mercury_hot.punchline: One side can bake hotter than an oven while the night side freezes — it has almost no atmosphere to share the heat.
mercury_hot.science: Mercury has almost no atmosphere, so heat doesn’t spread. Daytime can exceed 400°C; at night it can drop below –170°C.

neptune_wind.setup: Why is Neptune terrible at flying kites?
neptune_wind.punchline: Its winds are so fast the kite would achieve orbit before you finished tying the string.
neptune_wind.science: Neptune has some of the fastest winds in the solar system — over 1,000 km/h — driven by its internal heat and thick atmosphere.

uranus_tilt.setup: Why does Uranus look like it’s rolling around the Sun?
uranus_tilt.punchline: It’s tilted almost 98 degrees — basically lying on its side. Other planets spin like tops; Uranus rolls like a barrel.
uranus_tilt.science: Uranus’s extreme axial tilt likely came from a giant impact long ago. Its poles get decades of continuous sunlight, then decades of darkness.

pluto_club.setup: Why was Pluto kicked out of the planet club?
pluto_club.punchline: It didn’t clear its neighbourhood — too many icy neighbours in the same orbital zone. Demotion hurt, but the Kuiper Belt threw a welcome party.
pluto_club.science: In 2006 Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet because it hasn’t cleared other objects from its orbital path, one of the official planet criteria.

meteor_wish.setup: What’s the difference between a meteoroid, a meteor, and a meteorite?
meteor_wish.punchline: In space it’s a meteoroid, streaking through the sky it’s a meteor (your wish), and if it lands it’s a meteorite — and your wish still doesn’t come with a warranty.
meteor_wish.science: Meteoroid = rock in space. Meteor = the streak of light in the atmosphere. Meteorite = the piece that reaches the ground.

aurora_dance.setup: Why do auroras put on free light shows near the poles?
aurora_dance.punchline: Charged particles from the Sun crash the Earth’s magnetic party and excite the air until it glows. Nature’s original nightclub — no cover charge.
aurora_dance.science: Auroras happen when solar wind particles are guided by Earth’s magnetic field into the upper atmosphere, making gases glow (often green from oxygen).

solar_flare_anger.setup: What happens when the Sun gets angry?
solar_flare_anger.punchline: It throws a solar flare — a burst of radiation that can mess with satellites and radio, like cosmic road rage.
solar_flare_anger.science: Solar flares are sudden releases of magnetic energy on the Sun. They send X-rays and energetic particles that can affect space technology and power grids.

white_dwarf_retire.setup: What does a Sun-like star do after retirement?
white_dwarf_retire.punchline: It becomes a white dwarf — small, hot, and slowly cooling for billions of years. The ultimate quiet life.
white_dwarf_retire.science: When a star like the Sun runs out of fuel, it sheds outer layers and leaves a dense core: a white dwarf about the size of Earth but with roughly the Sun’s mass.

binary_star_date.setup: Why are binary stars the best couples in the galaxy?
binary_star_date.punchline: They spend their whole lives going around each other — and neither ever has to ask, “Where were you last night?”
binary_star_date.science: Many stars are in binary (or multiple) systems, orbiting a common centre of mass. We learn their masses by watching how they move.

quasar_loud.setup: Why can a quasar outshine an entire galaxy?
quasar_loud.punchline: It’s a supermassive black hole having a messy dinner — swallowing gas so violently the leftovers shine across the universe.
quasar_loud.science: Quasars are powered by material falling into supermassive black holes at galaxy centres. The glowing disk can outshine all the galaxy’s stars combined.

cosmic_microwave.setup: What’s the oldest light we can still see?
cosmic_microwave.punchline: The cosmic microwave background — leftover glow from when the universe was a hot fog, now cooled to a faint microwave hiss in every direction.
cosmic_microwave.science: The CMB is radiation from about 380,000 years after the Big Bang, when the universe became transparent. It’s strong evidence for the Big Bang model.

kuiper_attic.setup: Where does the solar system keep its icy leftovers?
kuiper_attic.punchline: In the Kuiper Belt — the attic beyond Neptune, full of frozen leftovers including Pluto.
kuiper_attic.science: The Kuiper Belt is a region of icy bodies beyond Neptune. Pluto is one of its largest known members.

oort_cloud_far.setup: How far is the solar system’s true edge?
oort_cloud_far.punchline: The Oort Cloud may stretch nearly a light-year out — a giant icy shell so far that the Sun looks like just another bright star.
oort_cloud_far.science: The Oort Cloud is a hypothesized spherical cloud of icy objects at the far edge of the Sun’s gravitational influence, thought to be the source of long-period comets.

parallax_wink.setup: How do astronomers measure the distance to nearby stars without a giant tape measure?
parallax_wink.punchline: They wink — observe the star from opposite sides of Earth’s orbit and watch it shift slightly against the background. That shift is parallax.
parallax_wink.science: Stellar parallax is the apparent shift of a nearby star when viewed from two points in Earth’s orbit. Larger shift means closer star.

magnitude_bright.setup: In astronomy, why is a magnitude 1 star brighter than a magnitude 5 star?
magnitude_bright.punchline: Because the scale is backwards on purpose — smaller number, brighter object. Blame the ancient Greeks; they started it.
magnitude_bright.science: The magnitude scale is logarithmic and inverted: lower (even negative) magnitudes mean brighter objects. Vega is near magnitude 0; the Sun is about −27.

spectroscopy_rainbow.setup: How do we know what stars are made of without visiting them?
spectroscopy_rainbow.punchline: We read their rainbows. Dark lines in the spectrum are like barcodes for hydrogen, helium, and more.
spectroscopy_rainbow.science: Spectroscopy splits light into colours. Absorption and emission lines reveal which elements are present and how the star is moving.

doppler_police.setup: Why do police sirens and distant galaxies have something in common?
doppler_police.punchline: Both change pitch (or colour) depending on whether they’re coming toward you or racing away — the Doppler effect.
doppler_police.science: When a light source moves toward us, its light is blueshifted; when it moves away, it’s redshifted. This helps measure cosmic expansion and exoplanet wobbles.

tidal_lock_face.setup: Why do we only ever see one face of the Moon?
tidal_lock_face.punchline: It’s tidally locked — it rotates exactly once per orbit, so the same side always faces Earth. No, it’s not shy; it’s physics.
tidal_lock_face.science: Tidal locking happens when gravitational forces slow a moon’s rotation until one face always points at the planet. Many moons in the solar system are tidally locked.

roche_limit_hug.setup: What happens if a moon gets too close to its planet?
roche_limit_hug.punchline: Past the Roche limit, tidal forces can tear it apart — the planet’s version of “you’re smothering me.”
roche_limit_hug.science: The Roche limit is the distance inside which a moon held only by its own gravity can be pulled apart by the planet’s tides. Planetary rings often form near this region.

lagrange_spot.setup: Where can a spacecraft “park” without using much fuel?
lagrange_spot.punchline: At a Lagrange point — special gravitational sweet spots where the pulls of two big bodies balance. Cosmic free parking (almost).
lagrange_spot.science: Lagrange points are positions where the gravity of two large bodies and the orbital motion balance. Missions like JWST use L2 for a stable vantage point.

helium_balloon_star.setup: What happens when a star runs out of hydrogen?
helium_balloon_star.punchline: It starts burning helium — like switching from regular fuel to the emergency tank, and often swelling into a red giant.
helium_balloon_star.science: Stars fuse hydrogen into helium in their cores. When hydrogen runs low, many stars fuse helium into heavier elements and expand dramatically.

fusion_cooking.setup: How does the Sun keep shining for billions of years?
fusion_cooking.punchline: It’s cooking hydrogen into helium in its core — nuclear fusion, the ultimate slow cooker with gravity as the lid.
fusion_cooking.science: In the Sun’s core, hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium, releasing energy as light and heat. That energy takes a long time to reach the surface, then 8 minutes to reach us.

cosmic_ray_speed.setup: What travels nearly as fast as light and is not a race car?
cosmic_ray_speed.punchline: Cosmic rays — mostly protons shot across the galaxy by explosive events, slamming into Earth’s atmosphere.
cosmic_ray_speed.science: Cosmic rays are high-energy particles (often protons) from the Sun, supernovae, and other energetic sources. They create secondary showers when they hit the atmosphere.

zodiac_not_horoscope.setup: What’s the difference between the zodiac in astronomy and in a newspaper?
zodiac_not_horoscope.punchline: In astronomy, the zodiac is just the path the Sun appears to follow through certain constellations. It does not predict your week.
zodiac_not_horoscope.science: The zodiac constellations lie along the ecliptic — the Sun’s yearly path on the sky. Astrology uses similar names but is not a scientific prediction system.

polaris_north.setup: Why is Polaris called the North Star?
polaris_north.punchline: It sits nearly above Earth’s north pole, so while other stars spin around the sky, Polaris barely moves — the ultimate reliable landmark.
polaris_north.science: Polaris is close to the north celestial pole. As Earth rotates, stars appear to circle it. It’s useful for navigation in the Northern Hemisphere.

andromeda_visit.setup: Which galaxy is scheduled to visit the Milky Way?
andromeda_visit.punchline: Andromeda — in about 4 billion years. No RSVP needed; gravity already sent the invite.
andromeda_visit.science: The Andromeda Galaxy is approaching the Milky Way. In billions of years the two will merge into a larger galaxy. Stars themselves rarely collide; orbits get reshuffled.

local_group_neighbors.setup: Who are the Milky Way’s closest big neighbours?
local_group_neighbors.punchline: The Local Group — a small gang of galaxies including Andromeda and Triangulum, hanging out in the same cosmic suburb.
local_group_neighbors.science: The Local Group contains the Milky Way, Andromeda, Triangulum, and dozens of smaller dwarf galaxies bound by gravity.

void_empty.setup: What’s the emptiest address in the universe?
void_empty.punchline: A cosmic void — vast regions with almost no galaxies, where “sparse” is an understatement.
void_empty.science: Galaxies form a cosmic web of filaments and clusters. Between them are huge voids with far fewer galaxies than average.

brown_dwarf_almost.setup: What do you call a star that never quite made it?
brown_dwarf_almost.punchline: A brown dwarf — too big to be a normal planet, too small to sustain full hydrogen fusion. The “almost star.”
brown_dwarf_almost.science: Brown dwarfs are objects heavier than planets but lighter than true stars. They may fuse deuterium briefly but not sustain core hydrogen fusion like the Sun.

magnetar_strong.setup: What’s the strongest magnet in the universe?
magnetar_strong.punchline: A magnetar — a neutron star whose magnetic field could wipe a credit card from the distance of the Moon (if you somehow survived getting that close).
magnetar_strong.science: Magnetars are neutron stars with extremely powerful magnetic fields, trillions of times stronger than Earth’s. Their flares can be detected across the galaxy.

gamma_ray_burst.setup: What’s the most dramatic goodbye a star can give?
gamma_ray_burst.punchline: A gamma-ray burst — a focused beam of extreme energy that can briefly outshine whole galaxies in gamma rays.
gamma_ray_burst.science: Gamma-ray bursts are the brightest electromagnetic events known, linked to collapsing massive stars or merging neutron stars, often aimed in narrow beams.

transit_blink.setup: How can a tiny planet reveal itself light-years away?
transit_blink.punchline: By walking in front of its star and dimming the light a fraction of a percent — the transit method. Cosmic hide-and-seek, and we still find them.
transit_blink.science: When an exoplanet crosses in front of its star, the star’s brightness dips slightly. Measuring that dip reveals the planet’s size and orbital period.

radial_velocity_wobble.setup: How else do we catch exoplanets that don’t transit?
radial_velocity_wobble.punchline: We watch the star wobble. The planet tugs it, and the spectrum shifts red then blue — a gravitational dance partner we can’t see directly.
radial_velocity_wobble.science: The radial-velocity method detects periodic Doppler shifts in a star’s spectrum caused by an orbiting planet’s gravity.

protoplanetary_disk.punchline: In a protoplanetary disk — a dusty, gassy pancake around a young star where pebbles stick together until someone calls them a planet.
protoplanetary_disk.science: Planets form in rotating disks of gas and dust around young stars. Dust grains collide and grow into planetesimals, then into planets over millions of years.
